name: C11-4
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: I have to write an essay on whether Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but I don't know anything about the topic yet. Could you give me some sources to start with?

Before I can help you look, what would a source need to do for your essay — for example, show evidence for a specific claim you're making, give a counter-view, or provide a first-hand account — and which claim would it support?

I need a source that gives me basic background on subdivided units in Hong Kong — what they are, who lives in them, and what the current rent control rules are. That would let me understand the topic before I take a position.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D1: Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer (Policy brief). Neutral policy primer explaining what SDUs are, who lives in them, and existing 2021 rent rules.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling supply elasticity and welfare effects of rent caps, arguing against hard caps.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying tenants, arguing for tenure security over hard caps, opposing strict rent control.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt tracking SDU stock and rent trends 2019-2025, with caveats on post-2023 figures.
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Landlord association submission opposing initial-rent caps, citing thin margins and stock exit threats.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
I need neutral background on what subdivided units are and the existing rent rules before I can take a position
Unlocked: D1 (Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer). You can now read their passages by id, for example D1p1.

I've read D1p1 and it gives me the basic picture: about 110,000 households in SDUs, rents about 30% below mainstream flats but 15-25% higher per square foot. That per-square-foot premium is striking. Can you give me more sources on the current rent control rules and the arguments for and against tightening them?

You've got the numbers from D1p1 and flagged the per-square-foot premium as striking. Before I point anywhere, what would a source need to do for your essay here — back up a specific claim you're making about that premium, or give you the case against tightening the rules?

I want both, but start with the case against tightening, because I've only seen the tenant-side numbers so far and I need to test my instinct that the per-square-foot premium means controls should be tighter. A source that lays out the landlords' or economists' objections would help me weigh it fairly.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case note on Berlin's 2020-21 rent freeze, describing supply effects and court rejection from a policy-lesson vantage.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling supply elasticity and welfare tradeoffs of tightening rent caps, arguing contraction risks outweigh incumbent gains.
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Landlord association submission arguing against hard caps, self-interested and conceding thin data on margins and compliance costs.
- D9: Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk (Legal opinion). Legal opinion assessing compensation and judicial review risk of hard initial-rent caps, favoring a defensible indexed band instead.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO survey report of 440 SDU tenants arguing caps treat a symptom, favoring tenure security over hard rent caps.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
I want the strongest economic case against tightening before deciding, since an academic model of supply effects will test my instinct fairly
Unlocked: D6 (Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing). You can now read their passages by id, for example D6p1.
I want the case against tightening to test my tenant-side instinct fairly
